memos.headline: Momentum Bifurcation: S05/S03/S09 Lead While S08/S01/S04 Lag Badly on Relative Strength
memos.body: I see a clear two-tier market as of January 9. The strongest technical setups are S05 (at its 52-week high, +86% over 26 weeks, RSI 69 but not yet extreme) and S09 (within 0.6% of highs, steady +4.2% over 4 weeks, RSI 61), both showing dominant relative strength versus SPY. S03 is surging with +9.2% in a single week and +5.8% 4-week relative strength, though RSI at 69.2 and a 6% premium to the 50-day mean suggest a near-term pullback risk. On the weak side, S08 has an RSI of 27.2—deeply oversold—with -7.9% 4-week relative strength and a -4.9% gap below its 50-day mean, which could set up a tactical bounce but the trend is clearly broken short-term. S01 sits 8.7% below its 200-day mean and 19.5% off its high, confirming a persistent downtrend I want no part of.

views.note: At 52-week highs with +29% 12-week relative strength vs SPY and massive trend; would reassess on a close below 310 (roughly the 50-day area).
Near highs with healthy RSI of 61, +6.2% 12-week relative strength, and well above both moving averages; invalidated below 118.
Strong momentum with +9.2% weekly return and leading relative strength, but RSI 69.2 and 6% above 50d mean raise pullback risk; would buy a dip toward 235.
Healthy trend near highs with RSI 58.6 and +5.2% 4-week relative strength; a close below 315 would change my view.
Massive 26-week gain of +58% and 39.5% above 200d mean screams extended; near highs but flat 4-week relative strength suggests momentum is stalling.
RSI 27.2 is deeply oversold and could trigger a mean-reversion bounce, but -7.9% 4-week relative strength and -4.9% vs 50d mean mean the trend is broken; need a reclaim of 270 to turn constructive.
Middling RSI of 49.7 and flat 4-week relative strength; above 200d mean but 10.7% off highs with no clear catalyst in the chart.
Negative 12-week return of -6.7%, -11.5% relative strength vs SPY over 12 weeks, and sitting right at the 200d mean with no upside momentum.
Down 19.5% from highs, 8.7% below 200d mean, and -9.7% 12-week relative strength—a clear downtrend I won't fight until price reclaims 150.
The 42.6% drawdown from 52-week high is alarming despite a recent 4-week bounce of +4.8%; sitting flat to the 200d mean with -9.2% 12-week relative strength, this is a show-me story.

memos.headline: S10 and S05 Show Durable Earnings Power; S02 and S09 Face Margin Compression
memos.body: I see a clear bifurcation in this universe between names with expanding margins and accelerating revenue versus those suffering earnings deterioration. S10 stands out with 62.5% YoY revenue growth, a 56.0% net margin, and only $8.47B in total debt — the cleanest earnings profile in the group. S05 also impresses at $102.35B revenue (+15.9% YoY) with a 34.2% net margin and minimal leverage ($14.79B debt), while S04 delivers 35.7% net margins on 18.4% revenue growth. On the other end, S02's net income collapsed 61.2% YoY to just $2.35B on a razor-thin 2.1% margin despite 12.2% revenue growth, signaling severe cost or mix headwinds against $80.14B of debt. S09 is the only name with negative revenue growth (-5.2%) and declining earnings (-12.3%), and I would need to see a revenue inflection before getting constructive.

views.note: 62.5% revenue growth, 56% net margin, and negligible leverage of $8.47B make this the strongest earnings compounder in the universe; a margin decline below 45% would change my view.
15.9% revenue growth with 34.2% net margin and low debt of $14.79B demonstrate durable, high-quality earnings power.
18.4% revenue growth and 35.7% net margin on manageable $43.21B debt; I'd reassess if revenue growth decelerates below 10%.
$180B revenue with 13.4% growth and 38.2% net income growth are solid, but 11.8% net margin leaves limited room for error on $55.1B of debt.
86.4% net income growth is impressive but $90.68B in total debt and only 7.9% revenue growth suggest the earnings jump may not be sustainable without top-line acceleration.
Steady 21.2% margin and 20% earnings growth, but only 3% revenue growth limits upside conviction; need to see top-line reaccelerate.
Revenue declining 5.2% YoY with net income down 12.3% and an 8.8% margin on $32.82B debt signals deteriorating fundamentals.
Net income collapsed 61.2% YoY to a 2.1% margin despite 12.2% revenue growth, with $80.14B in debt — classic cash-flow compression I refuse to pay for.

31% net margin and 8.8% revenue growth are respectable, but $427.2B in total debt dwarfs the rest of the universe and constrains upside.

memos.headline: Fed Easing Cycle Intact With Benign Inflation and Stable Labor Market – Favor Duration-Sensitive Growth, Constructive on Banks
memos.body: I see the Fed firmly in an easing regime: the upper bound sits at 3.75%, down 75bp over the past year and 50bp over the last three months, with the effective rate at 3.72%. Headline CPI is running at 2.7% y/y, comfortably below the fed funds rate, which gives the Fed room to continue cutting if the labor market softens further—unemployment at 4.40% is up 30bp y/y but has been flat the last three months, suggesting a slow-motion cooling rather than a sharp deterioration. The 10y yield at 4.18% is down 50bp y/y while the 10y-2y spread has steepened to +70bp (up 31bp y/y), a classic early-to-mid easing configuration that benefits duration assets and banks' net interest margins. A regime change would require either a CPI print re-accelerating above 3.5% y/y or unemployment jumping above 4.7%, which would shift the call from 'orderly easing' to either 'stagflation pause' or 'recession panic.'

views.note: Duration-sensitive growth benefits most from continued Fed easing and a 50bp y/y decline in the 10y yield.
Banks gain from a steepening curve (+70bp 10y-2y spread, up 31bp y/y) supporting net interest margins in an easing cycle.
Cyclicals face mixed signals: easing policy is supportive but unemployment drifting higher (+30bp y/y) caps upside conviction.
Staples lose relative appeal as the easing cycle favors risk assets, but stable unemployment keeps defensive demand from collapsing.
Rate-sensitive sectors should re-rate positively as the Fed has cut 75bp over the past year with further easing likely given 2.7% CPI.
Energy typically underperforms in a slowing-growth easing regime where demand expectations moderate alongside rising unemployment.

memos.headline: Limited Sentiment Signal Across Universe; S10 Negative Reaction Already Priced, S09 Reg FD Filing Warrants Monitoring
memos.body: I see very little actionable sentiment differentiation across the universe this week. The dominant theme is executive/director turnover (S08, S06, S04, S01, S02, S09, S07), which is noise absent further context on whether departures are voluntary or forced. S10 stands out with a -3.2% price reaction to its Nov 19 earnings 8-K, but that move is now nearly two months old and likely fully digested. S09 is the most active filer with three 8-Ks since mid-November, including a Reg FD disclosure on Jan 7 that could signal a proactive narrative shift—worth watching for tone change in media coverage. S07's Jan 6 filing combining officer changes with bylaw amendments is mildly unusual and could attract governance-focused negative coverage, though I have low conviction without GDELT tone data to confirm.

views.note: The -3.2% earnings reaction is stale at nearly two months old and likely priced in; no fresh catalyst.
Three filings in quick succession including a fresh Reg FD disclosure suggest management is proactively shaping narrative, a potential positive tone inflection.
Combined officer departure and bylaw amendment filing may attract negative governance-focused media tone, though conviction is low without confirming GDELT data.
Two director/officer change filings in a month are mildly elevated turnover but carry no clear directional sentiment signal.
Officer change plus shareholder vote submission is routine corporate governance activity with no discernible tone shift.
Single officer departure filing in mid-December is standard and unlikely to move sentiment.

memos.headline: Elevated Policy Uncertainty Persists Despite Calm Credit Markets; Oil Weakness Signals Demand or Supply-Side Geopolitical Shift
memos.body: I note a striking divergence: the Economic Policy Uncertainty Index sits at 474.73, up 34% over three months, even as VIX has fallen to 15.45 and HY OAS has tightened to 2.76%. This tells me markets are pricing benign credit conditions while the policy backdrop—likely driven by ongoing trade/sanctions rhetoric and energy policy shifts—remains structurally elevated. WTI at $57.74, down nearly 9% over three months, could reflect either weakening global demand tied to China slowdown or incremental supply from eased sanctions enforcement; either interpretation carries geopolitical weight. S09 filed a Reg FD disclosure on Jan 7, which in this environment I read as potentially pre-positioning around policy-sensitive guidance, and S03's November 8-K similarly warrants monitoring. Until I see concrete new export controls or sanctions escalation, I treat the uncertainty as a headwind for policy-exposed names but not yet a systemic risk.

views.note: Recent Reg FD filing suggests management is proactively communicating amid policy uncertainty; watching for sanctions or trade-related disclosures.
November 8-K Other Events filing during a period of rising policy uncertainty keeps me on the sideline until the nature of the disclosure is clarified.
Tight HY spreads and falling VIX suggest benign near-term conditions for names without direct geopolitical exposure; favoring domestically oriented credits.
With WTI down ~9% over three months and policy uncertainty elevated 34%, energy-exposed names face a dual headwind from demand weakness and potential sanctions-related supply shifts.
Steepening yield curve (+15bp over 3m) and low VIX favor duration-sensitive or growth-oriented names absent direct geopolitical risk; a new round of export controls would change this view.
